docs.title: Writing an MCP backend that validates ACH JWTs
docs.text:
Context first: the end-to-end trust path (forwarder mint → LiteLLM gateway → backend verify, including the extra_headers: ["authorization"] opt-in LiteLLM requires) is documented in JWT Forwarder. This runbook focuses on the backend-side verifier.

ACH's Forwarder mints a short-lived Ed25519 JWT on /mcp/<name> when a BackendIdentityPolicy (BIP) with spec.forwardIdentityJWT=true targets the named MCP server. This page describes how a backend operator implements the verifying side.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text: Aspect Value Reference Signing algorithm EdDSA (Ed25519) FWD-07 Header kid Stable id of the signing slot FWD-08 iss Forwarder ACH_BASE_URL (HTTPS-only) FWD-10 sub <owner-email> Hub §9.1 email Mirrors sub; additive, omitted when empty Hub §9.1 groups LiteLLM team aliases; additive, omitted entirely when the resolved set is empty — see The groups claim Hub §9.1 aud mcp:<bare-name> on /mcp/<bare-name> Hub §9.1 exp - iat 120 seconds FWD-07 nbf Not emitted Hub §9.1 jti Not emitted Hub §9.1 + §20 JWKS endpoint <iss>/.well-known/jwks.json Hub §9.2 JWKS Content-Type application/jwk-set+json RFC 7517 §8.5.1 JWKS Cache-Control public, max-age=3600 Hub §9.2 JWK shape kty=OKP, crv=Ed25519, alg=EdDSA, use=sig RFC 8037

docs.title: Recommended verification posture
docs.text:
1. Pin the algorithm. Reject anything other than alg=EdDSA on the JWS header. Never accept alg=none. Never trust the token's own alg value to pick a verifier — pin it before parsing.
  2. Resolve kid against a fresh-enough JWKS. Cache the JWK Set but refresh on kid miss; the Forwarder rotates with a publish- overlap-revoke flow (≥24h overlap), so a backend that holds a stale view of the JWKS for up to 1h is correct by design.
  3. Validate iss, aud, exp. iss is fixed per Forwarder install. aud is fixed per route (a backend that serves multiple <name>s accepts a small allowlist).

ACH does NOT emit nbf (intentionally — with a 120 s exp it adds only clock-skew risk; exp is the sole time bound). Verify iss, aud, exp only — do NOT require nbf. ACH also emits no jti. 4. Do NOT trust sub as identity unless your security model matches ACH's. sub carries the bare <owner-email> (no namespace prefix) — useful for audit, NOT authorization. The legacy <namespace>/<email> form is gone (pre-release hard-cut); do not split sub on /. Key on iss + sub.

docs.title: Handling the groups claim
docs.text: groups is optional — read it as an array of strings and treat an absent claim as an empty set, never as a verification failure. Don't fail verification if the claim is present but malformed; drop it and treat the caller as ungrouped instead. Key authorization decisions on the team-alias values themselves. For how pk_/ek_ resolve into the set, see the groups claim table in the Forwarder JWT reference — this runbook does not restate the resolution rules.

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text: A runnable, stdlib-only Go reference lives at test/e2e/mcp-echo/. The verifier is in test/e2e/mcp-echo/jwt/verify.go; the JWKS cache is in test/e2e/mcp-echo/jwt/jwks.go. Both files are ~150 lines and ship with their unit tests next to them — copy-and-adapt rather than import-as-library.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• kid missing from header — the Forwarder always emits one; a missing kid means you parsed a JWT minted by someone else.
  • Backend hot-loop on JWKS endpoint — refresh on miss, not on every request. The Forwarder's Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 is your hint.
  • Accepting alg=none — jwt.Parse(...) defaults vary by library; pin the algorithm explicitly.
  • LiteLLM strips Authorization by default — when ACH proxies through LiteLLM's MCP gateway (the default /mcp/<name> route), the gateway drops the caller's Authorization header before calling the backend. Register the backend with extra_headers: ["authorization"] so LiteLLM propagates the forwarder-minted JWT through to your MCP server. Without this the backend sees no token and 401s every request, and LiteLLM surfaces tools=[] even on healthy servers. ACH's scripts/cluster.sh hydrate_fixtures registers the e2e demo-mcp-echo server with this opt-in already in place.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
ACH runs as one image, ghcr.io/ackstorm/ach, started in a different mode per Deployment. Postgres holds ACH's state; LiteLLM serves the models and tools; Dex connects your identity provider.

 CRDs ──reconcile──▶ operator ──rows + NOTIFY──▶ Postgres ◀── read + LISTEN ──┐
                       │ (content service                                     │
                       │  runs beside it)                                     │
                       ▼                                                      │
                     LiteLLM ◀── forwarder ◀── tools (Claude Code, Codex, …)  │
                       ▲            │                                         │
                       └──────── platform-api ◀── ach-cli, console ──────────┘
                                    │
                                   Dex ──▶ your identity provider
Mode Role operator Reconciles the ACH resources, fetches content, writes LiteLLM access groups, teams and budgets, and projects everything into Postgres. content-service Serves fetched content to ach-cli. Runs as a second container in the operator Pod by default. platform-api Sign-in (an OAuth 2.1 server in front of Dex), keys, hydrate manifests, admin endpoints and the web console. forwarder The data path: checks the caller's credential, tags the request for budgets, and passes it to LiteLLM with the caller's own LiteLLM key. Mints per-backend identity tokens for MCP and A2A. gateway Optional. One address in front of platform-api, forwarder and content service. migrate Runs the Postgres schema migrations.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Component Used for Kubernetes Runs ACH; the resources are CRDs. Postgres ACH's source of truth: keys, Environments, content index. Back it up: keys cannot be re-created from the CRDs. Valkey Credential cache and sign-in state. LiteLLM (1.108 or later) Models, MCP servers, A2A agents, budgets. ACH holds its master key. Dex Connects any identity provider through one OIDC interface.

docs.title: Request path
docs.text:
1. A tool sends a request with an ACH credential to the forwarder.
  2. The forwarder resolves the credential to a person (and an Environment for an ek_), removes it, and adds the caller's own LiteLLM key and budget tags.
  3. LiteLLM checks the key's team and access groups and serves the request.
  4. For an MCP server or A2A agent with a BackendIdentityPolicy, the forwarder adds a short-lived token naming the caller.

The full contracts are in the JWT Forwarder guide.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: ACH decides which person or workload may use which models, tools and agent context, and delivers that context into their coding tools. It sits between your identity provider (through Dex) and LiteLLM.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
The central object. One Environment binds three things, reviewed together in one pull request:

  • Runtime: the models, MCP servers, A2A agents and guardrails its users may call, resolved against LiteLLM.
  • Context: the plugins, skills, prompts and artifacts written into a user's workspace.
  • Access: the LiteLLM teams (authorizedTeams) whose members may use it, and an optional spend ceiling (budget).

An Environment is Available once its content is fetched and its LiteLLM access group is in sync.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Term What it is Login ach-cli login signs you in through your company's identity provider. Your tools then act as you. Personal key (pk_) The key behind your login. ACH manages it; you rarely see it. Environment key (ek_) A key for one Environment, for an agent, a CI job or a script. Created with ach-cli keys create <environment>, shown once. It can expire, be suspended, resumed and revoked. Key exchange A pod trades its Kubernetes ServiceAccount token for a short-lived token acting for one Environment. No key is stored in the pod. KeyGrant The resource an admin writes to allow a key exchange: which ServiceAccount may act as which person in which Environment.

When your identity provider refuses you (for example, you left the company), your login and every Environment key you own stop working, within a day. This needs a Dex connector that asks the identity provider on refresh (Google, GitLab, Microsoft, GitHub and others); with SAML, an admin revokes the keys.

docs.title: Content
docs.text:
Kind What it is Plugin A Claude Code-style plugin (commands, skills, agents, hooks, MCP config). PluginMarketplace A repository of plugins, listed by its marketplace.json. Skill One agent skill: a directory with a SKILL.md. SkillMarketplace A repository of skills, discovered by its directory layout. Prompt One prompt file. Artifact Any other file or directory delivered to the workspace.

Content comes from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, S3, Google Cloud Storage or HTTP, and is refreshed on an interval.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text: ach-cli environment hydrate <environment> writes an Environment's content and MCP configuration into Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode or Pi. It records what it wrote, keeps your local edits, and environment uninstall removes exactly what it installed.

docs.title: Runtime access
docs.text: Term What it is Forwarder The ACH endpoint your tools call for models (/v1, /gemini), MCP servers (/mcp/<name>) and A2A agents (/a2a/<name>, or as an MCP server at /a2a/<name>/mcp). It checks your credential and passes the request to LiteLLM. BackendIdentityPolicy Tells the forwarder to send an MCP server or A2A agent a short-lived token naming the caller. Without one, the backend receives no identity. Shell team A LiteLLM team that allows nothing by itself. Each key lives in one, so it reaches only what its Environments grant. LiteLLMConnection How ACH reaches LiteLLM and where its master key is.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text: Three ceilings apply independently: per person (covering their login and every Environment key they own), per Environment, and per Environment key. LiteLLM enforces them; the request that crosses a ceiling is served and the next one is refused.

docs.title: Editions
docs.text:
ACH ships as one image, ghcr.io/ackstorm/ach, and one console. The Enterprise code is always in the image; it runs only when you enable it.

Core Enterprise (enterprise.enabled: true) Licence Apache-2.0 Core plus code under the ACKstorm Enterprise License Operator, platform API, forwarder, content service, gateway, console yes yes Overview from LiteLLM: spend, tokens, latency, allowance, request outcome, spend by key, usage by model yes yes Overview generation evidence: signals, input/output ratio, cache-read share, top apps, tool uses, recent sessions no yes ach classifier (conversation classification) no yes Classification results, Traces and sessions no yes Cost, Performance, Reliability, Runtime, Skills & context, Workloads analytics no yes

docs.title: Enabling Enterprise
docs.text:
Set it in the Helm values:

enterprise:
  enabled: true

The chart passes it to platform-api and the classifier as ACH_ENTERPRISE. Enabling the Enterprise features, in any environment, requires a signed agreement with ACKstorm, evaluation included. Running the image with Enterprise disabled needs none.

docs.title: With Enterprise disabled
docs.text:
• Every /platform/observability/* route (traces, sessions, context, workloads, cost, latency, performance, classification) answers 403 enterprise_only.
  • ach classifier exits with a message that it is an Enterprise feature.
  • platform-api refuses to start when ACH_OBSERVABILITY_CLICKHOUSE_URL, ACH_OBSERVABILITY_THANOS_URL or ACH_CLASSIFIER_TAXONOMY_FILE is set.
  • The chart keeps the classifier and platformApi.observability values but renders nothing from them, so turning Enterprise on is the single value above.
  • The console lists the Enterprise pages as "Enterprise only" and its Overview is the LiteLLM one.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: The core is under the Apache License 2.0. The code under ee/, ui/src/ee/ and cmd/ach/ee.go is under the ACKstorm Enterprise License (ee/LICENSE, ui/src/ee/LICENSE). You may read that code and redistribute it inside the official images; using it requires an agreement with ACKstorm.

docs.title: Choose a topology
docs.text:
The chart's defaults give a working install: one public rule to the gateway, one replica of each component, and content-service inside the operator Pod. This page covers the choices beyond that: how traffic reaches ACH, how to run more replicas, and how to collect metrics.

You need a running install, or the values.yaml of one you are preparing; see Install ACH with Helm.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Deployment Service and port Replicas ach-operator ach-operator-metrics:8080, metrics only Always 1 content-service, in the ach-operator Pod by default ach-content-service:8082 1; more when standalone ach-platform-api ach-platform-api:80 Any number ach-forwarder ach-forwarder:80 Any number ach-gateway ach-gateway:80 Any number

docs.title: Through ach-gateway
docs.text:
The gateway is a reverse proxy with a fixed route table and no logic of its own. Send all public traffic for the ACH host to the Service ach-gateway on port 80.

With the chart's Ingress:

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  host: ach.example.com
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600"   # long model and MCP streams
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: 32m         # large prompts and attachments
  tls:
    - hosts: [ach.example.com]
      secretName: ach-tls

With the Gateway API, leave ingress.enabled: false and write the route yourself:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: ach
  namespace: ach
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: <your-gateway>
      namespace: <gateway-namespace>
      sectionName: https
  hostnames: [ach.example.com]
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /}
      backendRefs:
        - name: ach-gateway
          port: 80

docs.title: Without the gateway
docs.text:
Use this only when your edge must treat paths differently, for example with separate timeouts or firewall rules. Set gateway.enabled: false and reproduce the gateway's routes in your own Ingress or HTTPRoute, all on one host:

Path Service /platform/ ach-platform-api:80 /content/ ach-content-service:8082 /v1/, /gemini/, /mcp/, /a2a/ ach-forwarder:80 /.well-known/opencode ach-platform-api:80 /.well-known/ (everything else) ach-forwarder:80 /v2/model/info (exact) ach-forwarder:80 / ach-platform-api:80

The /.well-known/opencode rule must win over /.well-known/. Do not route /metrics.

docs.title: Content-service: sidecar or standalone
docs.text:
Content-service serves the plugin and skill files that the operator fetches into a cache volume. By default it runs as a second container in the operator Pod and shares a ReadWriteOnce volume with it. That is one replica, and installing an Environment pauses while the operator Pod restarts.

To run several replicas, give the cache a ReadWriteMany volume and split content-service out:

operator:
  cache:
    size: 20Gi
    accessMode: ReadWriteMany
    storageClassName: efs-sc        # any ReadWriteMany class
contentService:
  standalone: true
  replicas: 3

On an existing install this needs a new volume, because Kubernetes does not allow changing the access mode or class of a PersistentVolumeClaim. Delete the claim ach-operator-cache as part of the change; the operator fetches everything again.

docs.title: Replicas
docs.text:
platformApi: {replicas: 2}
forwarder: {replicas: 3}
gateway: {replicas: 2}
  • These three keep no state of their own, so any number works. The chart adds no PodDisruptionBudget and no anti-affinity; add them yourself if you need them.
  • During a rollout the old Pod serves until the new one is ready, and then lets open requests finish for shutdown.timeoutSeconds, 120 seconds by default.
  • Keep operator.replicas at 1.
  • A change such as a new Environment reaches every replica within a few minutes.

docs.title: Metrics and dashboards
docs.text:
Each component serves /metrics without authentication on its Pod port: 8080 for the operator, platform-api and the forwarder, 8082 for content-service. Keep it inside the cluster. The operator, platform-api and forwarder Pods and the content-service Service carry prometheus.io/scrape annotations.

With the Prometheus Operator:

metrics:
  serviceMonitor:
    enabled: true
    labels: {release: kube-prometheus-stack}   # must match your Prometheus selector
  prometheusRule:
    enabled: true
    labels: {release: kube-prometheus-stack}
  dashboards:
    enabled: true
    namespace: monitoring      # where the Grafana sidecar looks

serviceMonitor and prometheusRule fail the install on a cluster without the Prometheus Operator resource definitions. The dashboards are ConfigMaps: if they do not appear in Grafana, its sidecar is not watching the namespace they are in, and nothing reports an error.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n ach get deploy,svc,ingress
curl -fsS https://ach.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server | jq .issuer
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://ach.example.com/metrics      # 404

The first curl prints your ACH address, and /metrics answers 404.

docs.title: Configure sign-in
docs.text:
Every person signs in to ACH through Dex: from ach-cli login, the web console, OpenCode, and the MCP sign-in of Claude Code and Codex. This page sets up the Dex client, and decides who is an admin, which teams a user joins, and what budget and key limit a new user gets.

You need Dex running with a connector to your identity provider; see the prerequisites. The values on this page go in the values.yaml of the install, and take effect with helm upgrade.

docs.title: The Dex client
docs.text:
Register a client for ACH in the Dex configuration:

staticClients:
  - id: ach
    name: ACH
    secretEnv: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET
    redirectURIs:
      - https://ach.example.com/platform/oauth/as-callback

Give ACH the same client through extraEnv:

extraEnv:
  - name: ACH_DEX_ISSUER_URL
    value: https://auth.example.com
  - name: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_ID
    value: ach
  - name: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: {name: ach-dex-client-secret, key: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET}

ACH_DEX_ISSUER_URL must equal the issuer of the Dex configuration character for character.

ACH asks Dex for the scopes openid email profile offline_access groups. Dex must provide:

From Dex Why A refresh token (offline_access) ACH renews each session with it. Without one, sign-in fails email ACH identifies a user by email in teams, budgets and keys groups Only if you map groups to admins or teams below. The connector to your identity provider must send them

Dex keeps one refresh token per user and client, and ACH shares it across all the tools of a user. refreshTokens.validIfNotUsedFor in the Dex configuration therefore limits how long an idle user stays signed in.

docs.title: OAuth redirect hosts
docs.text:
Tools on the user's machine (ach-cli, OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex) receive the sign-in on a local address, which ACH always accepts. A web application that signs users in to ACH, such as the claude.ai MCP connector, needs its host listed:

platformApi:
  oauth:
    redirectHosts: [claude.ai]

Any application can register itself as a client, so list only hosts you trust to receive your users' sign-in. Removing a host cuts its clients off at once.

docs.title: Admins
docs.text:
Admins can see every Environment and key, set any user's budget and key limit, and revoke other people's keys. Nobody is an admin until you name one:

platformApi:
  admins:
    users:                         # emails
      - alice@example.com
    sso:                           # groups from your identity provider
      - platform-admins@example.com
List Matching A change takes effect users Exact, including upper and lower case: write the email as your identity provider sends it At the helm upgrade, which restarts platform-api. Sessions survive sso Ignores case At the user's next sign-in, or within an hour for a user who is signed in

docs.title: Team enrolment at login
docs.text:
An Environment names the teams that may use it. ACH adds each user to teams when they sign in:

platformApi:
  teams:
    default: [default]               # every user
    users:                           # email: extra teams
      alice@example.com: [data-team]
    sso:                             # identity-provider group: teams
      platform-engineers@example.com: [platform]

Teams live in LiteLLM and are named by their alias. ACH creates the team default itself and no other: create the rest in LiteLLM.

  • default needs at least one team. If a team in it does not exist, the sign-in fails with default team unreachable.
  • users and sso add teams and never block a sign-in: a team that does not exist yet is skipped and tried again at the next sign-in.
  • A user who is already signed in picks up new users and sso teams with ach-cli refresh.
  • Removing a line here removes nobody from a team. Remove the user from the team in LiteLLM.
  • A user reaches an Environment a few minutes after joining its team.

docs.title: Default budget and key limit
docs.text:
platformApi:
  userDefaults:
    maxBudget: 100         # USD; "" = no ceiling; 0 = refuse every request
    budgetDuration: "30d"  # the budget resets after this; "" = never
    maxKeys: 5             # environment keys one user may hold; 0 = none

Budget. One ceiling per person covers their own sessions and every environment key they own. maxBudget is given to a user at their first sign-in. Changing it later does not change the ceiling of users who already have one. Change one person's ceiling with:

ach-cli admin users budget alice@example.com --max-budget 200 --budget-duration 30d

Key limit. maxKeys applies to every user without a limit of their own, admins included, and a change applies to the next key anyone creates. Give one person a different limit with:

ach-cli admin users limits alice@example.com --max-keys 10

docs.title: Token lifetimes
docs.text:
Both are set through extraEnv:

Variable Default Minimum ACH_OAUTH_ACCESS_TTL 1h 1m ACH_OAUTH_REFRESH_TTL 720h 1h

ACH checks a session against Dex each time its access token is renewed. A shorter ACH_OAUTH_ACCESS_TTL ends the session of a user removed from your identity provider sooner, and asks Dex more often.

When your identity provider refuses a user, because the account is suspended or deleted there, their environment keys stop working until they sign in again. This needs a Dex version and a connector that report the refusal; the saml, oauth, keystone and authproxy connectors never do. With those, when someone leaves, also run:

ach-cli admin keys revoke --owner alice@example.com

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
ach-cli login https://ach.example.com --profile default
ach-cli whoami                    # your email, your budget, your key limit
ach-cli admin list teams          # works only for an admin

A user who is not an admin gets not_admin from the last command.

docs.title: Connect ACH to LiteLLM
docs.text:
LiteLLM stays the gateway to models, MCP servers and A2A agents. ACH decides who reaches which of them, and uses the LiteLLM master key to do it. This page points ACH at LiteLLM and lists what to configure inside LiteLLM.

You need LiteLLM 1.108.0 or later, reachable from the ACH namespace, and its master key in a Secret; see the prerequisites.

docs.title: What ACH writes in LiteLLM
docs.text:
ACH component Writes Operator For each Environment, an access group and a team ach-env-<name>. For each user, the link between their team ach-user-<email> and the Environments they may use. The budget of each Environment platform-api Users, their team memberships and their budget at sign-in, and one LiteLLM key for each user and each environment key Forwarder Nothing. It replaces the caller's ACH credential with that caller's own LiteLLM key and tags each request with the user, the Environment and the key, so LiteLLM applies the budgets

ACH never serves LiteLLM's own UI or admin API (/ui, /key/*, /health, /model/*). Publish LiteLLM on its own host for those.

docs.title: Point ACH at LiteLLM
docs.text:
Set litellmConnection in values.yaml:

litellmConnection:
  endpoint: http://litellm.litellm.svc.cluster.local:4000
  masterKeySecretRef:
    name: litellm-master-key
    key: master_key

The Secret must be in the ACH namespace. The chart gives the endpoint and the key to every component. The operator creates the resource LiteLLMConnection/default from these values when it starts: do not add one to your own manifests.

docs.title: What to configure in LiteLLM
docs.text:
• Models, MCP servers and A2A agents. Register them in LiteLLM. Environments refer to them by name.
  • Teams. Create the teams your Environments authorize, by alias. ACH creates only the team default.
  • Master key. With the LiteLLM Helm chart the value is masterkey, in lower case. A misspelt key makes that chart generate a random one, and every ACH call to LiteLLM then answers 401.
  • Guardrails attached to a team need a LiteLLM Enterprise licence. An Environment that lists guardrails on an unlicensed LiteLLM never becomes available. Budgets need no licence.
  • Model aliases. Use router_settings.model_group_alias in LiteLLM. ACH does not rename the model in a /v1 request.
  • MCP servers that check the caller's identity need extra_headers: ["authorization"] and allow_all_keys: true on their LiteLLM registration. Without them the identity token ACH adds does not reach the server, and its tool list is empty. Writing an MCP backend has the detail.

docs.title: Forwarder credential headers
docs.text:
The forwarder reads the caller's credential from these request headers, in order; the first one present decides:

forwarder:
  headers:
    - {name: x-ach-key, mode: resolve}
    - {name: x-api-key, mode: resolve}

This is the default. A list you set replaces it, so repeat the entries you keep.

Mode The header holds The forwarder resolve An ACH credential: a key or a session token Replaces it with the caller's own LiteLLM key passthrough A LiteLLM key Forwards it unchanged. The request has no ACH user and no ACH budget

Two common additions:

forwarder:
  headers:
    - {name: x-ach-key, mode: resolve}
    - {name: x-api-key, mode: resolve}
    - {name: x-goog-api-key, mode: resolve}         # Gemini clients that hold an ACH key
    - {name: x-genai-api-key, mode: passthrough}    # LiteLLM keys under a name of your own
  • An ACH key is recognised in any listed header, also a passthrough one, and never reaches LiteLLM.
  • authorization cannot be listed. Authorization: Bearer is read when no listed header is present: an ACH session token or an ACH key is replaced, and anything else passes to LiteLLM unchanged.
  • A request with no listed header and no Authorization credential answers 401.

platformApi.headers has the same shape and accepts resolve only.

docs.title: Gemini model prefix
docs.text:
A Gemini client asks for a model by its Google name, for example gemini-2.5-pro. LiteLLM often registers the same model with a prefix, such as gemini.gemini-2.5-pro. List the prefixes to remove:

forwarder:
  gemini:
    stripModelPrefixes: ["gemini.", "gemini/", "vertex_ai."]

The forwarder removes the first prefix that matches from the model name in a /gemini request. It leaves /v1 requests alone.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n ach get litellmconnection default       # READY is True
ach-cli admin list models                          # the models LiteLLM serves

Then send one request with an ACH credential:

curl -fsS https://ach.example.com/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(ach-cli token)" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model": "<a model of one of your Environments>", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}]}'

docs.text:

docs.title: Enable Enterprise features
docs.text:
The ACH image always contains the Enterprise code, and one Helm value turns it on. This page turns it on and configures its two parts: personal observability and the conversation classifier. Editions lists what each edition includes.

You need:

  • A signed agreement with ACKstorm. It is required to enable Enterprise in any environment, evaluation included.
  • A running ACH install.
  • Langfuse receiving the traces of your LiteLLM, and access to its ClickHouse database.

docs.title: What the switch changes
docs.text:
enterprise:
  enabled: true

With it on:

  • The console shows the Enterprise pages: Traces, the analytics pages, and the extra evidence on the Overview. Each person sees their own data.
  • The chart renders the platformApi.observability and classifier values below.

With it off, the chart keeps those values in your file and renders nothing from them.

docs.title: Observability values
docs.text:
platform-api reads each user's own traces from the Langfuse ClickHouse database, and can read LiteLLM metrics from a Prometheus-compatible query API.

platformApi:
  observability:
    clickhouseUrl: http://clickhouse.langfuse.svc:8123
    secretName: ach-observability-clickhouse
    projectIds: [default]                                  # Langfuse projects to read
    thanosUrl: http://thanos-query.monitoring.svc:10902    # optional
Value Notes clickhouseUrl Empty leaves the pages without data. When set, secretName and at least one entry in projectIds are required secretName A Secret in the ACH namespace with the keys ACH_OBSERVABILITY_CLICKHOUSE_USER and ACH_OBSERVABILITY_CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD thanosUrl Empty leaves the Performance page without gateway metrics. It reads LiteLLM series labelled user=<email>

Create a ClickHouse user for this, read-only, with access to the metadata columns and not to the text of conversations. On a replicated ClickHouse, create the user on every replica, or sign-in to ClickHouse fails now and then.

docs.title: Deploy the classifier
docs.text:
The classifier labels each finished work session with one category and writes the label to Langfuse as a score. The console shows how work divides across the categories.

classifier:
  enabled: true
  secretName: ach-classifier
  clickhouseUrl: http://clickhouse.langfuse.svc:8123
  projectId: default
  modelUrl: https://ach.example.com/v1     # an OpenAI-compatible address
  model: <a model of the classifier's Environment>
  langfuseUrl: ""                          # empty: label and log, write nothing
  onlyUser: ""                             # label only this user's sessions

The Secret named by secretName holds:

Key Content ACH_CLASSIFIER_CLICKHOUSE_USER, ACH_CLASSIFIER_CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD A ClickHouse user that can read input and output on events_full and SELECT from scores. Not the observability user ACH_CLASSIFIER_MODEL_KEY A key accepted at modelUrl ACH_CLASSIFIER_LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY, ACH_CLASSIFIER_LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY A Langfuse key pair. Required when langfuseUrl is set

Keep these in that Secret and never in extraEnv. extraEnv reaches every other component, and this ClickHouse user can read conversations.

Send the model calls through ACH: create an Environment for the classifier with one model and a budget, create an environment key for it, and use that key as ACH_CLASSIFIER_MODEL_KEY. The classifier's spend then counts against that Environment.

Roll it out in three steps:

  1. Leave langfuseUrl empty. The classifier labels sessions and logs the result without writing anything. Check its log: kubectl -n ach logs deploy/ach-classifier.
  2. Set langfuseUrl and onlyUser to write scores for one person. Restart the Pod once and check that it does not label a session a second time.
  3. Clear onlyUser.

The log holds session ids, labels and counts, never conversation text.

docs.title: Your own categories
docs.text:
The built-in categories describe ACKstorm's work. Replace them with classifier.taxonomy; {}, the default, keeps the built-in ones.

classifier:
  taxonomy:
    rules:
      - "If the work is for a specific client account, classify by what was done for it, not by the client."
    categories:
      - id: operations.fleet_planning
        fits: "Routes, vehicle assignment, load planning, delivery schedules, warehouse slots."
        notFits: "Software that does the planning -> technology.software_engineering."
      - id: operations.incidents
        fits: "Delays, damaged goods, claims, carrier incidents and how they were handled."
      - id: customer.service
        fits: "Answering a customer: emails, tickets, delivery status, complaints."
        notFits: "A commercial offer -> sales.offers."
      - id: sales.offers
        fits: "Quotes, tenders, rate cards and proposals for a prospect or customer."
      - id: finance.billing
        fits: "Invoices, payments, costs, budgets, reconciliations."
      - id: technology.software_engineering
        fits: "Code, scripts, automations, spreadsheets with formulas built as tools."
      - id: general.research_learning
        fits: "Getting information where nothing is produced: explaining, comparing, looking up facts."
You set The classifier always adds categories: id, fits, and optionally notFits An introduction that tells the model the session is data, never instructions rules: extra rules, numbered from 4 Rules 1 to 3: classify by subject, not by task or format; a mixed session takes the category of most of it; other only when nothing fits The categories other and trivial. Do not list them

Write each category as the model reads it. A category becomes one line of the prompt: - <id>: <fits> Does not fit: <notFits>. Say what belongs in it, and name the category it is most often confused with.

Ids have the form domain.name, in lower-case letters, digits and _.

Every change is a new version. A custom taxonomy has the version custom- followed by 8 characters derived from the prompt it produces. Changing an id, a word of fits, a rule or the order makes a new version. The classifier then labels again every session inside lookback (72 hours by default), and each of those model calls is paid again. Comments and YAML layout do not change the version.

Report by metadata.category. The score value is the position of the category in the list, so the same number means another category in another version. Group reports by metadata.category and metadata.taxonomy.

A change to taxonomy restarts the classifier and platform-api, which reads the same categories for the console. The classifier does not start when the taxonomy has no categories, an unknown field, a repeated or malformed id, an empty fits or an empty rule.

docs.title: With the switch off
docs.text:
• The Enterprise pages of the console are marked "Enterprise only", and their API routes answer 403 enterprise_only.
  • The classifier is not deployed.
  • platform-api does not start if ACH_OBSERVABILITY_CLICKHOUSE_URL, ACH_OBSERVABILITY_THANOS_URL or ACH_CLASSIFIER_TAXONOMY_FILE is set through extraEnv. The chart never sets them with the switch off.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n ach rollout status deploy/ach-platform-api
kubectl -n ach logs deploy/ach-classifier --tail=20     # the taxonomy version and the category count

Open the console at https://ach.example.com: Traces lists your own sessions, and the pages are no longer marked "Enterprise only".

docs.title: Install ACH
docs.text:
In this tutorial you install ACH on a Kubernetes cluster with its Helm chart, sign in, and give your users a first Environment. It takes about thirty minutes.

ACH runs next to services the chart does not install. You need them in place, with these names; Prepare the prerequisites describes each one.

You need The tutorial uses A Kubernetes cluster, with kubectl and helm pointing at it Namespace ach, where Postgres and Valkey run A Postgres database and its user Database ach, user ach, host ach-postgresql Valkey or Redis ach-valkey-primary:6379, without a password LiteLLM with at least one model, and its master key http://litellm.litellm.svc.cluster.local:4000 Dex, with a client for ACH and its secret https://auth.example.com, client ach with the redirect address https://ach.example.com/platform/oauth/as-callback An ingress controller and a certificate issuer Class nginx, cert-manager issuer letsencrypt A DNS name for ACH that points at the ingress ach.example.com ach-cli on your machine

Replace the names with your own as you go.

docs.title: 1. Create the Secrets
docs.text:
kubectl -n ach create secret generic ach-key-encryption-key \
  --from-literal=dek="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
kubectl -n ach create secret generic ach-credential-hash-pepper \
  --from-literal=pepper="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
kubectl -n ach create secret generic litellm-master-key \
  --from-literal=master_key='<LiteLLM master key>'
kubectl -n ach create secret generic ach-dex-client-secret \
  --from-literal=ACH_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET='<the secret of the Dex client>'
kubectl -n ach create secret generic ach-postgresql \
  --from-literal=password='<the password of the database user>'

The first two are generated here and must never change afterwards. Back them up.

docs.title: 2. Write the values
docs.text:
Save this as values.yaml, with your own email under admins:

litellmConnection:
  endpoint: http://litellm.litellm.svc.cluster.local:4000
  masterKeySecretRef:
    name: litellm-master-key
    key: master_key

platformApi:
  admins:
    users: [you@example.com]
  userDefaults:
    maxKeys: 5

genai:
  providerName: my-org

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  host: ach.example.com
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
  tls:
    - hosts: [ach.example.com]
      secretName: ach-tls

extraEnv:
  - name: ACH_BASE_URL
    value: https://ach.example.com
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: {name: ach-postgresql, key: password}
  - name: ACH_DB_URL
    value: postgresql://ach:$(DB_PASSWORD)@ach-postgresql:5432/ach?sslmode=disable
  - name: ACH_REDIS_ADDR
    value: ach-valkey-primary:6379
  - name: ACH_DEX_ISSUER_URL
    value: https://auth.example.com
  - name: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_ID
    value: ach
  - name: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: {name: ach-dex-client-secret, key: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET}

providerName is the name OpenCode users will sign in with. Choose it now: changing it later signs them out.

docs.title: 3. Install
docs.text:
Find the latest version of the chart:

helm show chart oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach | grep '^version:'

Render the chart with your values, then install it, with that version in place of <X.Y.Z>:

helm template ach oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach --version <X.Y.Z> \
  -n ach -f values.yaml > /dev/null
helm upgrade --install ach oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach --version <X.Y.Z> \
  -n ach -f values.yaml --wait --timeout 10m

The first command prints nothing when the values are complete. The second ends with STATUS: deployed and a summary of the install.

docs.title: 4. Check the install
docs.text:
kubectl -n ach get deployments

NAME               READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
ach-forwarder      1/1     1            1           82s
ach-gateway        1/1     1            1           82s
ach-operator       1/1     1            1           82s
ach-platform-api   1/1     1            1           82s

kubectl -n ach get litellmconnection default

NAME      READY   REASON   AGE
default   True    Synced   77s

READY is True once the operator has reached LiteLLM with the master key.

curl -fsS https://ach.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server | jq -r .issuer

https://ach.example.com

docs.title: 5. Sign in
docs.text:
ach-cli login https://ach.example.com

Press Enter to accept the profile name default, then choose 1 to open the browser on this machine. Sign in with your organisation account. The terminal continues when the browser says you are signed in. Then check who you are:

ach-cli whoami

User shows the email you listed under admins, and Auth shows session.

docs.title: 6. Grant a first Environment
docs.text:
An Environment names what a team may use: models, tools, plugins and skills. List the models your LiteLLM serves:

ach-cli admin list models

Save this as quickstart.yaml, with one of those models:

apiVersion: ach.ackstorm.ai/v1alpha1
kind: PluginMarketplace
metadata:
  name: ach
spec:
  type: github
  github:
    repo: ackstorm/ach
    ref: main
  refresh:
    interval: 1h
    maxStaleness: 24h
---
apiVersion: ach.ackstorm.ai/v1alpha1
kind: Environment
metadata:
  name: quickstart
spec:
  runtime:
    models:
      - <a model from the list>
  context:
    plugins:
      - ach-cli@ach
  authorizedTeams:
    - default
  description: |
    First Environment: one model and the ach-cli agent plugin.

The PluginMarketplace makes the plugins of the ACH repository available. The Environment gives one model and one of those plugins to the team default, which every user joins when they sign in.

kubectl -n ach apply -f quickstart.yaml
kubectl -n ach wait environment/quickstart --for=condition=Available --timeout=5m
ach-cli environment list

quickstart is in the list.

docs.title: 7. Hand over to a developer
docs.text:
Send your users the address https://ach.example.com. They follow Your first Environment from their own machine, and quickstart is the Environment they find there.

When you no longer need it, remove it:

kubectl -n ach delete -f quickstart.yaml

Deleting an Environment also revokes every environment key created for it.

docs.title: Install ACH with Helm
docs.text:
This page installs ACH on a cluster where the prerequisites exist: Postgres, Valkey, LiteLLM, Dex, an ingress controller and the Secrets.

For a first install with every step in order, follow the Install ACH tutorial.

docs.title: What gets deployed
docs.text:
One image, ghcr.io/ackstorm/ach, runs every component.

Object Purpose Deployment ach-operator Applies the ACH resources (Environments, plugins, skills) to Postgres and LiteLLM. Its Pod also runs content-service, which serves plugin and skill files Deployment ach-platform-api The API, the sign-in server and the web console Deployment ach-forwarder Carries model, MCP and A2A traffic to LiteLLM Deployment ach-gateway One Service, ach-gateway, in front of the three above Job ach-migrate-<revision> Creates and updates the database tables before each install and upgrade The ACH custom resource definitions Kept when the release is uninstalled, together with your resources

The operator reads ACH resources in the release namespace only, so Environments and the other resources go there.

docs.title: Write the values file
docs.text:
Start from this values.yaml and replace the hosts, names and emails. Every value it leaves out keeps its default; the Helm values reference lists them all.

litellmConnection:
  endpoint: http://litellm.litellm.svc.cluster.local:4000
  masterKeySecretRef:
    name: litellm-master-key
    key: master_key

platformApi:
  admins:
    users: [admin@example.com]
  userDefaults:
    maxBudget: 100           # USD per user for each budgetDuration
    budgetDuration: "30d"
    maxKeys: 5               # environment keys one user may hold

genai:
  providerName: my-org       # the name OpenCode users sign in with

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  host: ach.example.com
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
  tls:
    - hosts: [ach.example.com]
      secretName: ach-tls

extraEnv:
  - name: ACH_BASE_URL
    value: https://ach.example.com
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: {name: ach-postgresql, key: password}
  - name: ACH_DB_URL
    value: postgresql://ach:$(DB_PASSWORD)@ach-postgresql:5432/ach?sslmode=disable
  - name: ACH_REDIS_ADDR
    value: ach-valkey-primary:6379
  - name: ACH_DEX_ISSUER_URL
    value: https://auth.example.com
  - name: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_ID
    value: ach
  - name: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: {name: ach-dex-client-secret, key: ACH_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET}

What to know about these values:

  • The database, Valkey and Dex settings have no value of their own. They go in the top-level extraEnv, which the migration Job and every component except the classifier receive. A component's own extraEnv does not reach the migration Job.
  • $(DB_PASSWORD) is replaced by Kubernetes with the variable defined above it, so the password stays in its Secret.
  • ACH_BASE_URL is the public origin of this install, with https:// and no path. Sign-in, download links and the keys ACH creates in LiteLLM carry it. Do not change it after users have signed in.
  • genai.providerName is part of the credentials OpenCode stores. Changing it signs every OpenCode user out, so choose it once.
  • platformApi.admins is empty by default, and so nobody is an admin. Configure sign-in covers both ways to name admins.
  • platformApi.userDefaults.maxKeys is 0 by default: nobody can create an environment key until an admin allows it.
  • Do not add ACH_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY, ACH_CREDENTIAL_HASH_PEPPER, ACH_LITELLM_BASE_URL or ACH_LITELLM_MASTER_KEY to extraEnv. The chart sets them from the security and litellmConnection values.

docs.title: Render
docs.text:
Render the chart before you install. A missing required value fails here, with a message that names it.

helm template ach oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach --version <X.Y.Z> \
  -n ach -f values.yaml > /dev/null

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
helm upgrade --install ach oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach --version <X.Y.Z> \
  -n ach --create-namespace -f values.yaml --wait --timeout 10m

On a first install the forwarder may restart once or twice, until the operator has created the Secret ach-jwt-signing-keys.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run these in order; each depends on the one before.

# 1. Every Deployment is available
kubectl -n ach wait deploy -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ach \
  --for=condition=Available --timeout=5m

# 2. The operator created the signing keys and reached LiteLLM
kubectl -n ach get secret ach-jwt-signing-keys
kubectl -n ach get litellmconnection default        # READY is True

# 3. ACH answers on its public address
curl -fsS https://ach.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server | jq .issuer
curl -fsS https://ach.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json | jq '.keys | length'   # 1

# 4. A person can sign in
ach-cli login https://ach.example.com
ach-cli whoami

If a step fails, see Troubleshoot an ACH install.

docs.title: Agent credentials by token exchange
docs.text: The platform API reviews ServiceAccount tokens for POST /platform/keys/exchange through a cluster-wide system:auth-delegator binding the chart creates. Set API server audit level Metadata for tokenreviews, and bind the <release>-keygrant-editor ClusterRole (ach-keygrant-editor for release ach) to platform admins only. See Agent credentials by token exchange.

docs.title: Prepare the prerequisites
docs.text:
The ACH chart installs ACH only. This page lists what must exist before you install the chart, and the Secrets you create for it.

The examples use https://ach.example.com for ACH, https://auth.example.com for Dex, and the namespace ach.

docs.title: Kubernetes and Helm
docs.text:
• Kubernetes 1.27 or later, and Helm 3 with OCI support.
  • A StorageClass for the 10Gi cache volume of the operator. The default access mode is ReadWriteOnce; see Choose a topology for the case that needs ReadWriteMany.
  • Rights to create cluster-scoped objects: the chart creates the ACH custom resource definitions (*.ach.ackstorm.ai), ClusterRoles and ClusterRoleBindings.

The chart is oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach and the image is ghcr.io/ackstorm/ach (amd64 and arm64, public). Chart X.Y.Z runs image vX.Y.Z.

docs.title: Postgres
docs.text:
ACH keeps its state in Postgres. The operator writes it and every other service reads it.

  • Create one database and one user that owns it. The install creates the tables, so the user needs the right to create them.
  • ACH reads the connection from ACH_DB_URL in its full form: postgres://ach:<password>@<host>:5432/ach?sslmode=<mode>. A URL without the user, the port or the scheme stops the services at startup.
  • Percent-encode special characters in the password (/ as %2F, ? as %3F, # as %23, % as %25), or use a password of letters and digits.
  • Connect directly or through a pooler in session mode. ACH uses LISTEN/NOTIFY, which a pooler in transaction mode drops.
  • Use sslmode=require or stricter when Postgres is outside the cluster network.

LiteLLM needs its own, separate database.

docs.title: Valkey or Redis
docs.text:
Valkey holds the sessions of signed-in users and caches. One standalone instance is enough. If its data is lost, every user signs in again and the caches refill.

Variable Required Value ACH_REDIS_ADDR Yes host:port ACH_REDIS_PASSWORD No The password, from a Secret ACH_REDIS_TLS No true to connect with TLS ACH_REDIS_DB No Logical database, 0 by default

docs.title: LiteLLM
docs.text:
ACH controls access to a LiteLLM proxy and does not replace it.

  • LiteLLM 1.108.0 or later, with its own Postgres database, reachable from the ACH namespace. The chart default is http://litellm.litellm.svc.cluster.local:4000.
  • Its master key, which you store in a Secret (below).
  • Its own public host, if anyone needs the LiteLLM UI or admin API. ACH does not serve LiteLLM's /ui, /key/* or /health.

Connect ACH to LiteLLM covers what to configure inside LiteLLM.

docs.title: Dex
docs.text:
Users sign in to ACH through Dex, which connects to your identity provider.

  • One issuer URL that both the users' browsers and the ACH pods can reach. ACH reads <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration at startup and does not start without it.
  • A connector that issues refresh tokens. ACH renews every session with the user's Dex refresh token, and a sign-in without one fails.
  • A connector that sends the groups claim, if teams or admins should follow groups of your identity provider.
  • Persistent storage. With in-memory storage every Dex restart signs everyone out.
  • A client for ACH. Configure sign-in shows it.

docs.title: Ingress and TLS
docs.text:
• One public hostname for ACH with TLS. ACH_BASE_URL must be exactly this origin, for example https://ach.example.com.
  • The ingress must pass Cookie and Set-Cookie unchanged on /platform/oauth/, and allow long streaming responses on /v1/ and /mcp/.
  • Never publish /metrics.

The chart can create the Ingress, or you route to ACH yourself; see Choose a topology.

docs.title: Secrets to create
docs.text:
Create these in the ACH namespace before the install. The names of the first three are the chart defaults.

Secret Key Content ach-key-encryption-key dek Base64 of exactly 32 random bytes ach-credential-hash-pepper pepper Random, at least 32 bytes litellm-master-key master_key The LiteLLM master key Your choice, for example ach-dex-client-secret Your choice The secret of the Dex client for ACH Your choice, for example ach-postgresql password The password of the ACH database user Your choice, for example ach-valkey password The Valkey password, if it has one 
kubectl -n ach create secret generic ach-key-encryption-key \
  --from-literal=dek="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
kubectl -n ach create secret generic ach-credential-hash-pepper \
  --from-literal=pepper="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
kubectl -n ach create secret generic litellm-master-key \
  --from-literal=master_key='<LiteLLM master key>'
kubectl -n ach create secret generic ach-dex-client-secret \
  --from-literal=ACH_DEX_CLIENT_SECRET='<the secret registered in Dex>'

Create the first two once and keep them

A new value in ach-key-encryption-key makes every stored LiteLLM key unreadable. A new value in ach-credential-hash-pepper invalidates every ACH key. Back both up, and keep them out of anything that regenerates Secrets.

Do not create ach-jwt-signing-keys: the operator creates it on its first start.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n ach get secret ach-key-encryption-key ach-credential-hash-pepper \
  litellm-master-key ach-dex-client-secret
curl -fsS https://auth.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .issuer

The four Secrets are listed, and the issuer printed is the URL you will give ACH, character for character.

docs.title: Rotate the JWT signing keys
docs.text:
ACH signs two kinds of token with one Ed25519 key: the access tokens of signed-in users, and the identity tokens the forwarder adds for MCP and A2A backends. This page replaces that key without breaking the backends that check those tokens.

You need kubectl access to the ACH namespace, openssl and jq.

docs.title: When to rotate
docs.text:
• On the schedule your security policy sets. ACH does not rotate the key by itself.
  • At once, when the key may have leaked: use Emergency revocation.

A planned rotation takes a day. Backends keep the published keys for up to one hour, so the new key is published for 24 hours before ACH signs with it.

docs.title: Secret layout
docs.text:
The key is in the Secret ach-jwt-signing-keys in the ACH namespace. The operator creates it on its first start, and it is kept when the release is uninstalled.

Data key Content current.kid Name of the key ACH signs with current.seed Its 32-byte seed next.kid, next.seed The key that comes next. Present only during a rotation

https://ach.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json publishes the public key of current, and of next while it is set.

docs.title: 1. Generate the next key
docs.text:
NEXT_KID_B64=$(printf 'ach-jwt-%s' "$(date +%s)" | base64)
NEXT_SEED_B64=$(openssl rand -base64 32)

Keep both values until step 5, and treat the seed as a secret.

docs.title: 2. Add it as next
docs.text:
kubectl -n ach patch secret ach-jwt-signing-keys --type=json \
  -p="[{\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/data/next.kid\",\"value\":\"$NEXT_KID_B64\"},
       {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/data/next.seed\",\"value\":\"$NEXT_SEED_B64\"}]"

docs.title: 3. Check that both keys are published
docs.text:
curl -s https://ach.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json | jq -r '.keys[].kid'

It prints two names. The forwarder logs jwt signing keys reloaded when it reads the change.

docs.title: 4. Wait 24 hours
docs.text: Every backend must fetch the new public key before ACH signs with it. A backend that has not rejects the tokens signed after step 5.

docs.title: 5. Make next the current key
docs.text:
kubectl -n ach patch secret ach-jwt-signing-keys --type=json \
  -p="[{\"op\":\"replace\",\"path\":\"/data/current.kid\",\"value\":\"$NEXT_KID_B64\"},
       {\"op\":\"replace\",\"path\":\"/data/current.seed\",\"value\":\"$NEXT_SEED_B64\"},
       {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/data/next.kid\",\"value\":\"\"},
       {\"op\":\"add\",\"path\":\"/data/next.seed\",\"value\":\"\"}]"

An empty next.kid clears the slot.

The forwarder reads the change at once, and platform-api and content-service within about 90 seconds. From then on ACH refuses the access tokens signed with the old key. A user's tool gets a new one at its next renewal, within the hour; signing in again renews it at once.

docs.title: 6. Check the result
docs.text:
curl -s https://ach.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json | jq -r '.keys[].kid'

It prints one name, the new one.

docs.title: Emergency revocation
docs.text:
When the current seed may have leaked, do not wait:

  1. Generate a key as in step 1.
  2. Replace current.kid and current.seed directly, with the two replace operations of step 5.
  3. Expect up to one hour in which backends still accept tokens signed with the leaked key, and reject tokens signed with the new one, until they fetch the published keys again. ACH cannot shorten that hour.

Do not delete the Secret to replace the key. The operator creates a new one only when it next starts, and a component that restarts before that does not start.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
curl -s https://ach.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json | jq '.keys | length'   # 1
ach-cli whoami

whoami answers, and an MCP server that checks the identity token lists its tools.

docs.title: Upgrade ACH
docs.text:
An upgrade is one helm upgrade with a newer chart version and the same values file. This page gives the procedure, what Helm does during it, and what a rollback cannot undo.

You need the values.yaml of the running install and a backup of the ACH database. The database is small, and the upgrade does not touch the LiteLLM database.

docs.title: How an upgrade runs
docs.text:
1. Helm renders the chart, including the ACH custom resource definitions, which upgrade with the release.
  2. The Job ach-migrate-<revision> updates the database tables for the new version. If it fails three times, the upgrade fails and no component changes.
  3. The Deployments roll to the new image. The operator stops before its replacement starts, so changes to ACH resources wait for a moment. With content-service in the operator Pod, installing an Environment waits too.

With installCRDs: false, apply the resource definitions from the new chart's crd-sources/ directory yourself before the upgrade.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
NEW=<X.Y.Z>; OLD=<the running version>

# 1. Read the changelog, and compare the default values of both versions
diff <(helm show values oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach --version $OLD) \
     <(helm show values oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach --version $NEW)

# 2. Render with your values: a missing or removed value fails here
helm template ach oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach --version $NEW \
  -n ach -f values.yaml > /dev/null

# 3. Upgrade
helm upgrade ach oci://ghcr.io/ackstorm/charts/ach --version $NEW \
  -n ach -f values.yaml --wait --timeout 10m

In the comparison of step 1, look for:

  • A value you set that was renamed. Helm ignores a key the chart no longer reads, and says nothing.
  • A value that became required.
  • image.tag, if you set it yourself: raise it in the same change. Left unset, it follows the chart version.

The changelog marks every change that needs a step from you under Breaking. Versions can be skipped unless the changelog says otherwise: the database updates of every version in between run in order.

docs.title: With Flux or Argo CD
docs.text:
• Pin the exact chart version, such as 1.2.3. A range such as 1.x upgrades production, database included, without review.
  • Keep the Secrets in a unit that the ACH release depends on, so they exist before the first migration Job runs.
  • A retry setting retries a failed migration Job; it does not undo it. Read the Job's log before letting retries continue.
  • With Flux variable substitution, $(VAR) in extraEnv is safe, and ${VAR} is replaced by Flux.

docs.title: Migrations and rollback
docs.text:
The database only moves forward. helm rollback restores the previous components and leaves the tables as the newer version made them. Most versions run on newer tables; read the changelog before you roll back.

Three cases where a rollback needs more:

Rolling back Needs first Below 1.1.4 Apply 000028_drop_deletion_timestamp.down.sql from the ACH repository with psql. The rows that version removed do not come back Below the version that added key suspension and expiry Resume every suspended environment key and clear every expiry. The tables refuse to go back while such a key exists Below the version that added token exchange Revoke every environment key that was issued by token exchange

To run the database update yourself, set migrate.enabled: false and run the ACH image with args: [migrate] and ACH_DB_URL set.

docs.title: Values that must not change
docs.text:
Value A change breaks Content of the Secret behind security.keyEncryptionKey Every stored LiteLLM key becomes unreadable: users and environment keys get 401 until they are created again Content of the Secret behind security.credentialHashPepper Every ACH key stops being valid ACH_BASE_URL Sign-in for every user, the Dex redirect address, the download links of installed Environments and the MCP entries users' tools saved genai.providerName Signs every OpenCode user out The Secret ach-jwt-signing-keys Deleting it invalidates every access token in use, and components do not start until the operator has created a new one. Replace its keys with Rotate the JWT signing keys The database behind ACH_DB_URL All ACH state. Move the data, not only the address

You can rename the Secrets as long as their content moves with them.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n ach wait deploy -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ach \
  --for=condition=Available --timeout=5m
kubectl -n ach get litellmconnection default        # READY is True
kubectl -n ach get environment                      # AVAILABLE is True for each
ach-cli whoami

A Job that succeeded is deleted. If the upgrade failed at the migration, read its log with kubectl -n ach logs job/ach-migrate-<revision>.

OpenCode users who see errors right after an upgrade restart OpenCode (opencode service restart on OpenCode v2).
